segments.title: The Fog and the System: Setting Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried read of one of the great English novels.
Over this series, we'll be working through Dickens chapter by chapter, bringing the novel off the page and into the light.
Today we begin at the very beginning: the fog, the mud, and the fog again — and the institution that sits at the heart of it all, the Court of Chancery.
I'm joined by three remarkable people, each of whom brings something quite different to this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens critics of his generation.
Edmund reads Bleak House as a novel about moral character — about individual virtue and weakness tested to their limits.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who has spent his career studying the Victorian institutions Dickens was attacking.
James can tell us what the Court of Chancery actually was — and why that matters enormously for how we read this book.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive.
Oliver hears what Dickens wrote for the voice — the rhythms, the comedy, the moments when the prose itself becomes performance.
So — the opening paragraph of Bleak House.
Edmund, you've read these lines more times than you can count.
What do you hear in them that a first-time reader might miss?
What one hears, above everything else, is the audacity of the thing.
Dickens opens not with a character, not with an event, but with a single word: London.
A full stop. Then nothing but weather and moral implication for a page and a half.
And then he introduces his Megalosaurus — that extraordinary image.
"It would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
He is telling us, from the very first page, that London has reverted to something primordial.
That civilisation — law, commerce, the whole institutional edifice — is a thin crust over something ancient and chaotic.
That, to my mind, is not a political statement. It is a metaphysical one.
And what I'd add — speaking as someone who has stood in a recording booth with those sentences — is that the grammar is doing something extraordinary.
There are no main verbs for the first half-dozen sentences. Just nouns. Fragments.
"London. Michaelmas term lately over. Implacable November weather."
It reads like a telegram from the edge of the world.
There's no subject in those opening sentences because the fog is the subject — the fog is the governing force.
When I perform it aloud, I let those fragments land separately, each one like a footstep into deeper mud.
That's not literary analysis — that's just what the prose demands of the human voice.
I want to hold onto Edmund's word — primordial — because it captures something important about Dickens' strategy.
This fog is not decorative. It is doing specific institutional work.
Look at where Dickens places us next: inside the Court of Chancery itself.
And what a portrait it is.
"This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard."
That anaphora — 'which has its... which has its' — is the rhetorical structure of an indictment.
The real Chancery by 1852 had cases pending that had been active since the reign of George the Third.
Dickens was not exaggerating. He was, if anything, exercising restraint.
James is quite right about the legal specifics, and I shan't contest them.
But I would gently resist the idea that the novel's power is exhausted by its accuracy as social critique.
The fog serves a deeper purpose than exposing Chancery, important as that exposure is.
It is the atmosphere in which character is formed and tested.
The fog obscures — and what it obscures most dangerously is one's own moral bearing.
That, I submit, is why Jarndyce and Jarndyce can destroy Richard Carstone as surely as it destroys any estate.
The institution corrupts from within, not merely by consuming money, but by corroding the will.
What strikes me — and Edmund, I think you're circling this — is that Dickens actually makes the fog funny as well as dreadful.
There's that wonderful passage near Temple Bar — which, incidentally, was a genuine civic eyesore, a stone gate blocking Fleet Street — where Dickens goes superlative mad.
Listen to the architecture of this sentence.

"The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction, appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old corporation, Temple Bar."
Rawest. Densest. Muddiest. He stacks the superlatives like a comedian stacks a punchline.
And then 'leaden-headed old obstruction' — repeated — 'leaden-headed old corporation.'
The joke is in the echo. The institution is literally the same thing as the lump of masonry blocking the road.
Dickens the moralist and Dickens the music-hall comedian are the same man. Always.
Oliver's point about Temple Bar is worth dwelling on, because the geography here is precise.
Lincoln's Inn Hall was the actual seat of the Chancery court. Dickens is not inventing an institution — he is describing one that every reader in 1852 would have known personally, or feared.
And that passage I read earlier ends with a warning I find almost unbearably poignant.
"Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here."
That is Dickens quoting the practitioners themselves — the honourable men inside the system, advising suitors to stay away.
When the people who run an institution tell you to avoid it, you are dealing with something that has ceased, in any meaningful sense, to function.
That is not satire. That is reporting.
James's word — reporting — opens something I want to pursue.
Because Dickens doesn't just set his scene in the fog and leave us there.
Very early in the novel, he poses a question — a rhetorical, almost cosmic question — about connection across the social divide.
He asks: what connexion can there be between the grand house in Lincolnshire, the fashionable town house — and Jo, the crossing-sweeper, the outlaw with a broom?
That question — unanswered, left hanging in the fog — is in some sense the engine of the entire novel.
We'll be returning to it throughout this series.
For now — the fog has settled, the court is in session, and we've only just begun.

segments.title: The Corrupted Inheritance: Richard's First Gamble

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, where we read Dickens slowly, carefully, and with full attention to what he's doing and why it matters.
I'm your host, and today we're entering what I think is the novel's most devastating story — the ruin of Richard Carstone.
A young man of real promise, real charm, real feeling — consumed by degrees by the Chancery suit he was born into.
With me today are three readers whose company I would want for exactly this kind of reckoning.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moralist, and the reader among us most likely to hold Richard Carstone personally responsible for his own fate.
Professor James Blackstone — legal historian, whose knowledge of what Chancery actually was will keep the rest of us honest.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, Dickens reader extraordinaire, who has given voice to Richard's decline more times than perhaps he'd care to count.
Let's begin at the beginning — the moment Richard first reveals that his approach to studying law has nothing to do with law at all.
What strikes me first, every single time I read that passage, is the hesitation Dickens builds into the sentence itself.
Richard says he wants to study the law — and then he stalls, mid-sentence, before naming what he really means.
Listen to how Dickens writes it — and those dashes are doing everything.
"I should have my eye on the — hum! — the forbidden ground — and should be able to study it, and master it."
That "hum!" — that tiny, embarrassed noise — is one of the most damning stage directions Dickens ever inserted into reported speech.
Richard knows, even as he speaks, that he's rationalising.
The suit is the forbidden ground — forbidden because everyone who loves him has warned him away from it — and he's walking straight towards it, eyes wide open.
Oliver is right to land on that word — and I'd add that "master" is equally telling.
Richard does not say he wishes to understand the suit, or to seek justice through it.
He wishes to master it — as a man masters a horse he intends to ride to his own purposes.
This is the characteristic Dickensian irony: the very confidence that makes Richard appealing is what makes him vulnerable.
He believes his will is stronger than the institution.
It is a form of pride — not the monstrous kind, but the ordinary, entirely human kind that Burke would recognise as the besetting sin of the young.
And one notices, too, the cheerful, almost comical energy at the end — "peg away at Blackstone and all those fellows with the most tremendous ardour."
"Peg away" and "tremendous ardour" in the same breath — it is the language of a schoolboy planning to conquer mathematics.
Dickens gives us, with perfect economy, a young man who is entirely charming and entirely doomed.
I want to pause on what Richard is actually proposing here, because the institutional reality is rather grimmer than the rhetoric suggests.
The Court of Chancery in the 1840s was not a system that rewarded scrutiny from suitors.
It was a system that rewarded patience — or rather, the financial endurance to sustain patience across decades.
Richard's fantasy of "studying" his own suit from inside a solicitor's office reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of how the machine operated.
Jarndyce v. Jarndyce was not a case with moving parts a young clerk could monitor — it was a geological formation.
It had been accumulating for so long that the original point of dispute had been buried under generations of procedural sediment.
Richard thinks proximity is power.
Jarndyce already knows, with the knowledge of bitter experience, that proximity is poison.
And Jarndyce himself eventually gives us the most precise account of what that poison does — the clinical stages of a Chancery victim.
Oliver, will you read that passage?
Gladly — and I want to say before I read it that this is one of the great sustained sentences in the whole novel.
"A young man so unfortunate cannot at first believe — who could? — that Chancery is what it is.
He looks to it, flushed and fitfully, to do something with his interests and bring them to some settlement.
It procrastinates, disappoints, tries, tortures him; wears out his sanguine hopes and patience, thread by thread;
but he still looks to it, and hankers after it, and finds his whole world treacherous and hollow."
"Thread by thread" — that's the phrase I can never get past without stopping.
It's not a blow — it's an unravelling.
And then that ending — "treacherous and hollow" — Jarndyce isn't describing the court.
He's describing what the world looks like to a man whose faith has been systematically destroyed.
What Dickens gives Jarndyce here is something very rare in the novel — genuine structural sympathy, offered without sentimentality.
Jarndyce does not excuse Richard.
He says "we must not be hard on him" — which implies that hardness would be a comprehensible response.
He is arguing, with painful precision, that a good man placed in these circumstances would also break.
That is not a comfortable thought for those of us inclined to locate the tragedy in Richard's individual character.
And yet — and this is where I think Dickens is most subtle — the novel does not entirely surrender that judgement either.
Richard is not simply a victim.
He is a man who chooses, at each juncture, the wrong door — and Dickens, with his moral imagination fully engaged, shows us both the choosing and the compulsion behind it.
There's something very important in Jarndyce's arithmetic that I don't want to let pass.
He says good men would be "vitally changed and depreciated" — and then he counts down: within three years, within two, within one.
"Within three years — within two — within one."
That descending rhythm isn't rhetorical decoration — it's a very precise description of how institutional damage accelerates.
The longer you're entangled, the faster the disintegration proceeds, because hope is finite and the court is not.
The historical record bears this out with some consistency.
The suitors who lasted longest in Chancery were rarely the ones who emerged vindicated.
They were the ones who had simply forgotten what they were fighting for.
And Richard himself, in Chapter Thirty-Seven, gives us a declaration that reads almost like a parody of resolution — except it's entirely sincere, which makes it all the more terrible.
Yes — and I've performed that speech many times, and the challenge is always the same: how do you play a man who believes absolutely what he's saying, while everything around him contradicts it?
Richard says — and the voice is quite urgent here, quite high and clear —
"It can't last for ever. I am young and earnest, and energy and determination have done wonders many a time.
Others have only half thrown themselves into it. I devote myself to it. I make it the object of my life."
"I make it the object of my life" — each word landing separately, like footsteps down a corridor.
The awful irony is that Dickens tells us, just before this, that "his face, his voice, his manner, all showed that too plainly."
Esther can see the ruin already written in his body, even as he speaks of devotion and determination.
That gap between what Richard says and what Esther sees — that's the gap the whole tragedy lives in.
It is worth dwelling on the word "devote," because it carries a weight Dickens understood very well.
Devotion is a religious word.
Richard has not simply chosen a career strategy — he has chosen a faith, and the court is his idol.
The novel is full of false religions — Tulkinghorn's cold power, Skimpole's aestheticism, Mrs. Jellyby's telescopic philanthropy.
Richard's particular heresy is the worship of a future that will never arrive.
And it destroys him precisely because he brings to it exactly the qualities — energy, earnestness, commitment — that in any other context would have served him well.
That observation connects to something the narrator tells us in Chapter Thirty-Nine — a passage I find almost unbearably lucid as a piece of social analysis.
Richard cannot fight the suit directly — it's too vast, too abstract, too impersonal.
So he does what people do when institutions defeat them — he finds a human face to put on his grievance.
And that face, tragically, is Jarndyce's — the one man who has tried to protect him.
Dickens puts it with a precision that still strikes me as remarkable.
"Injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat."
"Shadows" and "substances" — that opposition is doing so much work.
The court is the shadow — intangible, unkillable, without a face.
Jarndyce becomes the substance — the available enemy, the one you can point at and say: there is where my ruin began.
This is the psychological mechanism of scapegoating, described with total clarity — in 1852.
I assigned myself that passage, and I confess it troubles me in ways I did not entirely anticipate when I first proposed a more character-centred reading.
The narrator here is not judging Richard — or rather, not only judging him.
The narrator is describing a mechanism — almost a law of moral physics.
And yet — and I want to insist on this — Dickens does not remove agency from Richard entirely.
Look at the phrase: "it is a justification to him in his own eyes to have an embodied antagonist and oppressor."
"A justification to him in his own eyes" — Richard is not merely deceived.
He is self-justifying.
There is a collaboration between the institution's malice and the individual's will to avoid the harder self-knowledge.
That is where I locate the tragedy — not in one or the other, but in that collaboration.
And then there's the passage Esther gives us in Chapter Fifty-One — which I find the hardest to read aloud, of any passage in the book.
Harder than the deathbed scenes, honestly, because it describes something still living but already undone.
Esther is watching Richard's forced hopefulness — the performance of optimism that has curdled into something awful.
"His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness,
had something so fierce in its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager,
and yet so conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched me to the heart."
"Fierce in its determination to be it" — that phrase makes me go very quiet every time.
The hopefulness is trying to be hopefulness.
It has lost its own nature and become an act of will — strained, exhausting, and transparent to everyone except Richard himself.
The sentence that follows may be, for my money, the finest in the entire novel.
"I say indelibly, for I felt persuaded that if the fatal cause could have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in that same hour,
the traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach, and disappointment it had occasioned him would have remained upon his features to the hour of his death."
Even victory would not have saved him.
The damage was no longer contingent on the outcome — it had become constitutional, written into the body.
This is where Dickens ceases to be a social reformer and becomes a tragic poet.
The wrong cannot be undone.
Which brings us, inevitably, to what Esther sees when she visits Richard in Chapter Sixty — the physical inventory of ruin.
Dickens gives us a list — thin, languid, slovenly, abstracted — and each adjective is doing something different.
Thin and languid are the body's failure.
Slovenly is the failure of self-presentation — Richard no longer performs the gentleman.
Abstracted is the most ominous — he is no longer fully here.
And then the eyes — "about his large bright eyes that used to be so merry there was a wanness and a restlessness that changed them altogether."
"A wanness and a restlessness that changed them altogether."
The eyes, in Victorian fiction, are where the soul lives.
And Richard's soul, Esther is telling us, has been changed past recognising.
And then Dickens delivers the final line of that passage — which, in any Dickens novel, would be remarkable.
In Bleak House, it lands like something from Greek tragedy.
Esther says she cannot call him old.
"There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away."
"A ruin of youth which is not like age."
Age has its own dignity, its own form.
What Richard has is something categorically different — a destruction without replacement, a collapse without the architecture of grief.
It's the worst thing Dickens can imagine happening to a young person.
And he makes you feel it — not just understand it, feel it — through Esther's eyes.
A ruin of youth which is not like age.
I think we might let that sentence stand as the close of this segment.
In our next section, we'll look at the agents of that ruin — Vholes, the law's most perfect instrument, and what Dickens means when he gives a predator such courteous manners.

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.
c1:p5.best_quote: This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance.

c1:p3.text:
The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the
muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction,
appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old
corporation, Temple Bar. And hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln’s Inn
Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in
his High Court of Chancery.
c1:p3.summary: The fog and mud are thickest at Temple Bar and Lincoln's Inn Hall, where the Lord High Chancellor sits in the High Court of Chancery at the heart of murk.
c1:p3.best_quote: The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction, appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old corporation, Temple Bar.

c16:p5.text:
What connexion can there be between the place in Lincolnshire, the
house in town, the Mercury in powder, and the whereabout of Jo the
outlaw with the broom, who had that distant ray of light upon him
when he swept the churchyard-step? What connexion can there have been
between many people in the innumerable histories of this world who
from opposite sides of great gulfs have, nevertheless, been very
curiously brought together!
c16:p5.summary: The narrator poses a rhetorical question about how the Dedlock world and Jo's marginal existence might be mysteriously connected, hinting at larger patterns of connection across social divides.
c16:p5.best_quote: What connexion can there be between the place in Lincolnshire, the house in town, the Mercury in powder, and the whereabout of Jo the outlaw with the broom, who had that distant ray of light upon him when he swept the churchyard-step?

c17:p62.text:
“If I went into Kenge’s office,” said Richard, “and if I were placed
under articles to Kenge, I should have my eye on the—hum!—the
forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it, and
to satisfy myself that it was not neglected and was being properly
conducted. I should be able to look after Ada’s interests and my own
interests (the same thing!); and I should peg away at Blackstone and
all those fellows with the most tremendous ardour.”
c17:p62.summary: Richard explains that by entering Kenge's law office, he could monitor the Chancery suit while ostensibly studying law, revealing that his interest in law is entirely instrumental to his obsession with the suit.
c17:p62.best_quote: If I went into Kenge's office...I should have my eye on the—hum!—the forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it

c35:p40.text:
“We WILL hope so, my Esther,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “and that it may not
teach him so too late. In any case we must not be hard on him. There
are not many grown and matured men living while we speak, good men
too, who if they were thrown into this same court as suitors would
not be vitally changed and depreciated within three years—within
two—within one. How can we stand amazed at poor Rick? A young man so
unfortunate,” here he fell into a lower tone, as if he were thinking
aloud, “cannot at first believe (who could?) that Chancery is what it
is. He looks to it, flushed and fitfully, to do something with his
interests and bring them to some settlement. It procrastinates,
disappoints, tries, tortures him; wears out his sanguine hopes and
patience, thread by thread; but he still looks to it, and hankers
after it, and finds his whole world treacherous and hollow. Well,
well, well! Enough of this, my dear!”
c35:p40.summary: Jarndyce describes the psychological trajectory of a Chancery victim: hope, disappointment, torture, and ultimate despair.
c35:p40.best_quote: A young man so unfortunate cannot at first believe (who could?) that Chancery is what it is. He looks to it, flushed and fitfully, to do something with his interests and bring them to some settlement. It procrastinates, disappoints, tries, tortures him; wears out his sanguine hopes and patience, thread by thread; but he still looks to it, and hankers after it, and finds his whole world treacherous and hollow.

c37:p72.text:
Poor dear Richard! He had indeed been thinking about it a good deal.
His face, his voice, his manner, all showed that too plainly.
c37:p72.summary: Richard declares his absolute commitment to resolving the Chancery suit, his intensity revealing his obsession.
c37:p72.best_quote: It can't last for ever. I am young and earnest, and energy and determination have done wonders many a time. Others have only half thrown themselves into it. I devote myself to it. I make it the object of my life.

c39:p44.text:
Yet the time is so short since his depreciation began that as he
saunters away, reluctant to leave the spot for some long months
together, though he hates it, Richard himself may feel his own case
as if it were a startling one. While his heart is heavy with
corroding care, suspense, distrust, and doubt, it may have room for
some sorrowful wonder when he recalls how different his first visit
there, how different he, how different all the colours of his mind.
But injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being
defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat;
from the impalpable suit which no man alive can understand, the time
for that being long gone by, it has become a gloomy relief to turn to
the palpable figure of the friend who would have saved him from this
ruin and make HIM his enemy. Richard has told Vholes the truth. Is he
in a hardened or a softened mood, he still lays his injuries equally
at that door; he was thwarted, in that quarter, of a set purpose, and
that purpose could only originate in the one subject that is
resolving his existence into itself; besides, it is a justification
to him in his own eyes to have an embodied antagonist and oppressor.
c39:p44.summary: The narrator analyzes how Richard's corruption has progressed: unable to combat the abstract suit, he has seized upon Jarndyce as a concrete enemy and embodiment of all his injuries, justifying himself with the logic of having an enemy.
c39:p44.best_quote: injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat

c51:p59.text:
His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his
despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in
its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so
conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched
me to the heart. But the commentary upon it now indelibly written in
his handsome face made it far more distressing than it used to be. I
say indelibly, for I felt persuaded that if the fatal cause could
have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in
that same hour, the traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach,
and disappointment it had occasioned him would have remained upon his
features to the hour of his death.
c51:p59.summary: Esther reflects deeply on the tragedy of Richard's forced optimism, which has worn itself into his face as permanent marks of anxiety and self-reproach that will outlast any resolution of the suit.
c51:p59.best_quote: His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched me to the heart.

c60:p96.text:
We sat down to dinner, and I had an opportunity of observing Richard,
anxiously. I was not disturbed by Mr. Vholes (who took off his gloves
to dine), though he sat opposite to me at the small table, for I
doubt if, looking up at all, he once removed his eyes from his host’s
face. I found Richard thin and languid, slovenly in his dress,
abstracted in his manner, forcing his spirits now and then, and at
other intervals relapsing into a dull thoughtfulness. About his large
bright eyes that used to be so merry there was a wanness and a
restlessness that changed them altogether. I cannot use the
expression that he looked old. There is a ruin of youth which is not
like age, and into such a ruin Richard’s youth and youthful beauty
had all fallen away.
c60:p96.summary: Esther observes Richard's alarming physical decline: he is thin, languid, slovenly, abstracted, with dull eyes instead of his old merry brightness, embodying a tragic ruin of youth.
c60:p96.best_quote: There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away.
